title: Are You Approachable?
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Prompted by a how-to-work-with-me user manual her new boss asked her team to complete, Muth Martinez asks how leaders are actually experienced by the people around them. Her argument is that unapproachability is almost never reported directly; it shows up as people holding back critique, deleting messages, and building workarounds to manage friction with the leader. She names four forms: strong opinions that pre-decide the conversation, intensity that reads as pressure, poor responses to feedback, and chronic unavailability. Because self-report is unreliable, she suggests reading behavioural signals such as whether people push back or merely align, and whether bad news reaches you early. The remedy is unglamorous repeated behaviour, like not cutting people off and following up on concerns, rather than declaring an open-door policy.
points: Unapproachability is rarely named to a leader's face; it surfaces as silence, withheld critique and organizational workarounds that make things look fine.
Strong opinions, intensity, defensive reactions to feedback and constant unavailability are four common faceless forms of the problem.
Leaders should read behavioural data, such as whether opinions get pushback or only agreement and how early bad news arrives, instead of trusting self-assessment.
Approachability is taught through slow repetition of small acts like asking follow-up questions and genuinely considering alternatives, not by declaring an open-door policy.
quotes: The workarounds do their job, and from your vantage point everything probably looks basically fine. But it’s quite easy to mistake “fine” for “good” when ultimately, they’re not the same thing.

It might be as subtle as consistently seeming distracted when someone is talking to you, or offering a solution before someone has had a chance to finish describing the problem. It might be unintentional, but in these moments, we signal that we have our own preferred stance and aren’t really open for anything different.

the other people in the room will certainly notice that, and eventually they’ll stop offering their own thinking altogether. At that point you’ve stopped being part of a team and rather designed a room full of people performing agreement.
Leaders who are genuinely approachable tend to get bad news when it’s still small enough that they can help do something about.

What works here is probably a lot less gratifying, in things like noticing when you’re about to cut someone off, in taking someone’s feedback with grace, in asking a follow-up question when someone shares a concern, and in actually considering an alternative approach. These are the actions that teach people, slowly and through repetition, that you’re approachable.
Most leaders aren’t trained to ask these kinds of questions directly. Which is, somewhat ironically, part of what makes them hard to work with.
